Alright, well first thing is, what are you going by as unemployment rate? If you mean those in the workforce, actively seeking employment, and still eligible for unemployment benefits, than sadly that number is most likely not as skewed to the down side as you think.

Unemployment statistics are notoriously hard to put in a perspective though with meaningful context. Even more so if you take it back a step to labor participation, where those who have stopped looking for work, students, and the retired can really fudge shit up. Like how it gets used now to say 'we are at the lowest level of labor participation in x years'... We have more and more retired people living longer, more and more people attending school full time, and believe it or not more people leaving careers to start families. So clearly labor participation cannot tell you a lot either without seeing how the number is arrived at.

Best way to understand the labor market, and where it is going, is in jobs gained and lost by an economy over a period. And then wage rates change. If jobs are being lost, but wages are going up, it means less demand for the available labor and something like government regulation, or the like, is fueling the shrinking of the labor force and making the economy contract ultimately. Wage rates going up, number of jobs increasing, means there is actual growth happening most likely as employers must compete for employees. Point ultimately is, employment rate statistics, and labor participation rate, are highly relative to their time, and need to be understood in that context.

I would say though that it is more a matter of chronic underemployment in the labor force (a far, far more serious problem in an economy than under employment actually), and leaving the workforce altogether in disgust, which is really manifesting how hurting the economy is right now.
